title: Everyday Work (Colossians 1:15–20)
transcript: Well, as Sue has said, it's Workplace Sunday, which is great because we've got the chance to think about some of the things the Bible says about our work. My day job is that I am a lawyer, and it's taken me quite a long time to learn that being in lawyer mode at home with your family is not always a good thing to do. And let me give an example of this. Just before my wife and I got married, I was looking at the words that you say in the wedding service, you know, "Will you love her, honor her, comfort her, and protect her?" And one of the things we do as lawyers is we pick over words. We like— we add words in, and we analyze words. So I was looking at the wedding service, and I was thinking, well, you know, there are going to be times I fail to love you, there are going to be times I fail to comfort you, and I suppose there are times I fail to protect you. And so, in perhaps the most unromantic moment ever, my suggestion was that in the wedding service, I would say, "I will use reasonable endeavors to love you. I will use reasonable endeavors to comfort you, and terms and conditions apply." So, that was not one of my best suggestions. So, if you will put up with me, we will do this together. And there are 3 things I'd like us to look at tonight, because if we're thinking about our work, The first thing we need to do is to get a solid grasp on the fact that Jesus' domain stretches everywhere, even to the places where we do our work. And when I say work, I don't just mean those of us who do paid work, because some of us do paid work in places, other of us, other of us do work that's unpaid, caring for members of the family. Some of us do work that is the work of applying to get a job, filling in job applications. But whatever our work is, the first thing we need to do is to have a firm grasp on the fact that Jesus's domain stretches everywhere, even to the place we do our jobs. So that's the first point. The second thing is I'd like to look at the fact that whenever we think about work for a short period of time, we'll realize that we are people who mess things up, and we often mess things up at work. And the glory we have is that the one in whose domain we work is is one who offers us forgiveness. And so that's a great comfort, and we'll look at that. And the final thing we'll do is we'll look at the fact that this forgiving God cares about even some of the small things, things that seem ordinary in the eyes of the world. And that's a glorious thing to look at. So let's look at the first point. If you can grab one of the Bibles, we're on page 1182. And if we want to ask our question, the question, does our work matter to God, it's important to realize that we work within his domain. So let's come back to Colossians chapter 1 and have a look at verse 16. It's talking about Jesus. For in him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or powers or rulers or authorities, all 'all things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together.' Did you see the 'alls' in that? Look at verse 16: 'For in him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or powers or rulers or authorities. All things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together.' So everything in heaven and earth was created through him and for him, and he is, in the words of verse 17, the one who holds all things together. He sustains it. So this is his world, and that includes the little parts of the world where we all do our jobs. So let me take an example. Some of us here will spend Monday to Saturday in retail, working in a shop. And that shop, that place, whether the owners like it or not, is part of Jesus' dominion. He is the rightful Lord of that shop. And as we've said, his dominion encompasses unpaid work too. So he's the rightful Lord of the place where you give your time to volunteer. So if we take seriously that Jesus' domain stretches everywhere, even to our work, Of course it matters what we do at our work. It's important. I'm going to put up a quote in a second from a man called Abraham Kuyper, and he was a really interesting man because he was a theologian and he was Prime Minister of the Netherlands. You don't often get that. And as well as being a theologian and Prime Minister of the Netherlands, he founded a university and he worked as a journalist and he founded a newspaper. So he was someone who had clearly thought through what it was to have faith in Jesus and work in the secular world. And this is a quote he said. He said, "There's not one square inch in the whole domain of our human life of which Christ, who is sovereign of all, does not cry, 'Mine.'" You see, this is Jesus's world, and the little parts that we work in are parts of his dominion. And get this up. And the little part of the world that I work in might be different from the little part of the world that you work in, but he has put us together as a body of believers who are all working in different places and serving him. So have a look at verse 18 again of Colossians chapter 1. See, it says, and he is the head of the body, the church. So you see, we are all doing this together. In this church, there's a massive range of different kinds of work that people do during the week. And just imagine how beautiful it would be if we went into our different places of work scattered across London saying, Lord, this work that you've put me in, this place, Lord, it's under your lordship. Guide me in my work and my time here. May I love you, may I love others in my time here. Wouldn't that be glorious if we were all doing that? Which brings us on to our next point, because again, whenever we start thinking about work, we begin to think, well, look, I've messed things up. I've really messed up a number of things at work. Which is why it is gloriously good news that the one whose dominion encompasses our whole work is the one who is the most forgiving and wonderful God we could imagine. Come back to me with a passage. Just look at the verses above what we read. Look, come back to me to verse 13, just before our reading. So it says, for he has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of the Son he loves, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. Because all of us, every one of us, are people who need to be, verse 13, rescued. If you need to be rescued, and I need to be rescued, we need to be rescued, we need a rescuer. And in Jesus, we have a rescuer who in verse 14 offers us the forgiveness of sins. So the one in whose world we work in, the one in whose domain this is, is one who welcomes us to come to him and seek forgiveness for the things that we mess up. Now, isn't that a comfort? You know, the one who is the ultimate boss The one who is our boss's boss, or the one who is our boss's boss's boss, or the one who is our boss's boss's boss, yet the ultimate boss, is one who we can run to for forgiveness when we mess things up at work. And the passage drills this home to us. Have a look at verse 19. Look at 19 and 20. For God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him, and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through his blood shed on the cross. Do you see that little word 'reconcile' in verse 20? This world needs reconciliation. It's in a mess. It's alienated from God, and it needs to be reconciled to him. But in Jesus, God conducts the biggest peacemaking mission that this world has ever seen. God the Father sends his Son Jesus to reconcile the world to him. And verse 20 tells us how he does it. Have a look at verse 20. He does it— the end of verse 20— by making peace through his blood shed on the cross. Gave his life for us on the cross to offer us forgiveness and the chance of peace and reconciliation. And so every part of his dominion however godless our workplaces might be, however messed up our workplaces might be, they are a place where he offers the chance for peace and reconciliation. And it actually goes beyond us, and I'm going to apply this to work, but let me take it in stages. If we were sending out mission partners to, say, Japan, we would want people who understood the Japanese language, We would want people who understood Japanese culture, who understood what Japanese people were into. And we would want people with a heart for Japanese people to know the peace and the reconciliation and the hope that is in Jesus. Now, what if we weren't sending mission partners to Japan, but we were sending mission partners to, say, software engineers in London? Well, who would we want? We would want someone who understands how software engineers in London think, We would want someone who understands the culture of software engineers in London, and we'd want someone who has a heart to say, I want these people to know the peace and the reconciliation and the hope that's found in Jesus. And so we want— if you're a software engineer in London, you might be the best-placed mission partner to, to reach the people. And after you've done that, you can come and fix my IT problems at home, but you might be well placed for that. There's a theologian called Darrell Cosden who wrote a book called The Heavenly Good of Earthly Work. And he said that sometimes we might need to self-consciously name ourselves as a missionary. So if your job is a lab technician, you might need to say, I am a missionary to lab technicians in London. Now, when this, when this point comes up, when the topic comes up of being a missionary, sharing Jesus's good news to the people around you, The thing that's often said is, "Well, you know, it's difficult at work. There's all kinds of restrictions on what I can and can't say. I'm limited in what I can and can't say." But that's true of all mission partners, isn't it? I mean, there are Christian mission organizations who send mission partners into all different places of the world, some of which are positively hostile to the Christian faith. And it does mean they need to be wise, needs to be wise about how they share the gospel, but it doesn't mean they don't go. And as each person is transformed, as, as, as lights are turned on, as people see the hope that's in Jesus, we will find that the environment around gets transformed bit by bit. Of course, there is loads of brokenness in the world, and one day Jesus will return and he will put all things right. But until he returns, there are good things that can be done as people go out from into their places. Let me give an example. There was a lovely Christian solicitor— there is a lovely Christian solicitor who is a very good friend of mine, and he did a case once where his clients received a letter, and his clients received a letter saying that his clients— alleging that his clients had copied the designs of another person. And my friend, he's a lovely Christian man, he prays about his work and he desires to do it with his heart set on God. So he's got this situation, his client has got a letter saying, "Look, you've copied our designs." And I read the letter he sent back to the other side, and it was beautifully graceful. Like, he acknowledged the good things in the people on the other side of the case. And he politely and respectfully set out response. You know, they'd threatened to sue his clients, and he said, "Well, you'd like to think about this and this." But it was done with grace, it was done with prayer. And 3 things happened in that case. First of all, the other side never sued his clients. There was no litigation. Secondly, the parties ended up collaborating. They worked together on something, they did something useful together, they did a joint project together. So far from suing each other, they did something creative together. And the third thing that happened is the other side started sending him a Christmas card each year. And as a lawyer, I can count on two fingers the number of Christmas cards I've had from my own clients. I have never, ever had a Christmas card from someone on the other side of the case. And this story, this thing that happened, These aren't organizations that any of us will have heard of. They're small companies. But in that little area of the world, in that tiny corner of the world, peace broke out. And it happened in large part because there was a prayerful man who decided to do his job, do his job with his eyes set on Jesus. And it could have been destructive. People could have ended up in the spiral of litigation. But he chose to commit his work to God. And seek a better way. So we've looked at the fact that Jesus's domain stretches everywhere, even to our work, and we've looked at the fact that Jesus offers forgiveness and reconciliation not just to us but to the world around us, which brings us on to the last point: that Jesus cares about things that might seem small in the eyes of the world. And there's lots of places we can go to, to highlight this, but we're just going to give some examples in the time we've got. And here's the first one. This is Matthew chapter 10, verse 42, on the screen. This is Jesus speaking. He says, if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones who is my disciple, truly I tell you, that person will certainly not lose their reward. So this is an example of Jesus caring even about a cup of cold water being given to someone who is one of his disciples. Now, what could be more fleeting than that? Like, if you drink a cup of water, you get thirsty again and you still need another one. But Jesus cares about it even though it's tiny in the eyes of the world. And I personally, I find this verse very helpful because there's many days at work where I feel I haven't done anything earth-shattering. In fact, Nearly all the days I have at work, I feel I haven't done anything earth-shattering. But I find this verse a great comfort to say, Lord, I know this hasn't been earth-shattering what I've done. I've tried to do it with my eyes set on you, and you are a God who cares even about a cup of cold water. I commit it to you. Because little things, things that seem small in the eyes of the world, still matter to him. I don't know if you've read this book, uh, The Great Divorce by C.S. Lewis. It's an imaginary bus journey to the edge of heaven. Okay, so C.S. Lewis imagines himself taking a bus trip to the edge of heaven, and there's this great scene in it where he sees this glorious figure approaching him. I mean, this figure bathed in light who is awesome and amazing, and people around her dancing. And he sort of says to his tour guide who's with him, he says, 'Who is that?' And his guide says, 'Oh, you won't have heard of her. Her name on earth was Sarah Smith, and she lived at Golders Green.' And he says, 'She is one of the great ones, but fame here and fame on earth are two different things.' You see how that gives value to things that we do that might seem small in the eyes of the world? They might be glorious in heaven. So we've looked at one example, the cup of cold water. Here's another example of some of the things within his dominion that comes to our work that might seem small, but he cares about. How about this one? This is Mark chapter 6, verse 3, and they're talking about Jesus, and they say, isn't this the carpenter? Isn't this Mary's son and the brother of James, Joseph, Judas, and Simon? Aren't his sisters here with us? So this is people talking about Jesus, and they say, "Isn't this the carpenter?" And as far as I know, you can't go to a museum or an art gallery anywhere in the world and see there, "This table was carved by Jesus during his earthly ministry," or, "This chair was made by Jesus 2,000 years ago." It's not on display anywhere. But he didn't waste his time doing it. It was stuff that he thought was important enough to work on. One of the ministry trainees here at All Souls, Will, made the point to me that this Jesus doing the work of the carpenter is the same one who Colossians has described in our passage as the one through whom and for whom all things have been made and in whom all things hold together. This glorious one who is the one above all things, who holds all of creation together, he knows what it's like to work, and he will never pass away. All good and beautiful things are from him. He lives forever, and he is the audience who sees our daily work even if nobody else notices, because he is the only audience that matters. So we've looked at how Jesus cares even about a cup of cold water. We've looked at how he worked as a carpenter. How about this one, this example? This is Isaiah chapter 40, verse 31. It says, but those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They will soar on wings like eagles. They will run and not grow weary. They will walk and not be faint. We sort of expect the crescendo to go the other way, don't we? You see, it goes— we'd sort of expect it to go walking, running, soaring. Yeah? And lots of the world focuses on the times that we soar, that we do something amazing. But I love the fact that this crescendo goes the other way. They will soar on wings like eagles, they will run and not grow weary, and it ends with, 'They will walk and not be faint,' because there is something beautiful and glorious about patient daily walking, even if it might seem boring in the eyes of the world. The fact that you might be filling in the same kind of spreadsheets that you filled in yesterday at work, or you might be washing the same kind of clothes that you washed yesterday, doesn't mean it's unimportant. There is something glorious about patient daily work, which brings us to a challenge for us. So here's the challenge for us: are we praying about our work? Because if we take seriously that everything we do is within his dominion and he cares about what we do at work, are we inviting Jesus into our work? And one really important way of integrating our faith in our work is to pray about our work, which is the challenge for us. Are there points within our working day where we are turning our mind to God and seeking his presence in the midst of our work? So that's the challenge for us. Are we praying about our work? Well, our time is up. We've looked at three things. We've looked at the fact that Jesus's domain stretches everywhere even to the little parts of the world where we do our work. We've looked at the fact that Jesus, the one whose dominion this is, is the one who offers peace and forgiveness to our work, to us. However messed up we are, however messed up our workplace is, there is always hope of forgiveness and peace and reconciliation in him. And finally, we looked at the fact that in his goodness and in his graciousness He cares about things that might be small or uneventful in the eyes of the world. He cares about the cup of cold water. He cares about carpentry work, even if it doesn't end up in art galleries or museums. And he cares about the patient walking, even when we don't saw. Let me close with a prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you that it is you who is Lord of this domain. Thank you that it is you, the one who offers forgiveness and peace and reconciliation, that is in charge even in our workplaces and in our lives. Thank you in your goodness and your graciousness that you care about things even when they're overlooked in the eyes of this world. So please help us in our work. Please help us to integrate our faith in you with our work, because there is no better thing than to be doing our work with you. So please help us to be prayerful about our work. Please be with us in our work. And as we offer all these prayers to you, Lord, we acknowledge that there is nothing in us that is good that you should listen to us. So dear Father, we dare not offer these prayers in our own name. We offer them in the name of the one who is worthy. We offer them in the name of your Son, our Savior Jesus Christ. Amen.
